tips.title: V = IR, and rearrange it carefully
tips.body: **V = I R.** To find current, $I = V \div R$; to find resistance, $R = V \div I$. The specification says you must **recall and apply** this, so it will not be given to you. Write it down before substituting anything.

tips.title: Ohmic means the graph is a straight line
tips.body: An **ohmic conductor at constant temperature** gives a **straight line through the origin** on a current–potential difference graph, because current is **directly proportional** to pd. A curve means the resistance is **changing**.

tips.title: Say potential difference, not voltage
tips.body: Questions are set using **potential difference**. You get credit for either term, but using the specification's word keeps your answer aligned with the mark scheme — and "pd" is an acceptable abbreviation once you have written it in full.

tips.title: A filament lamp heats up; a thermistor cools down
tips.body: A **filament lamp**'s resistance **increases** as it gets hotter. A **thermistor**'s resistance **decreases** as temperature increases. They move in **opposite** directions, which is exactly why they are examined together.

tips.title: A diode conducts one way only
tips.body: Current through a **diode** flows in **one direction only**; in reverse it has a **very high resistance**. Its graph is flat at zero one side of the origin and rises steeply the other.

why.matters:
You met $V = IR$ in Year 10. This is where it earns its keep. Resistance is the one of the three you can **design**: choose a length of wire, a material, or a component that changes with heat or light, and you have chosen the current for every potential difference.

Ohm's law says which components are predictable and which are up to something. A straight line through the origin means a resistor doing nothing but resist; a curve means the component is reacting to its own temperature, to the light, or to the direction of the current, and the shape of the graph is a fingerprint for what is inside.

examples.title: Why the mower is weaker at the end of a long lead
examples.body:
A cable reel is required practical 3 in a garden: resistance grows with length. The current goes out along the live core and back along the neutral, so a 50 m reel is 100 m of copper: about 1.21 Ω, against 0.12 Ω for a 5 m lead.

A mower drawing 10 A then loses $V = IR = 10 \times 1.21$, about 12.1 V of the 230, along the cable before it starts, and that energy warms the reel at $I^2R$, about 121 W. Left coiled, that is a 121 W heater in a tight drum, which is why the label says unwind it fully.

props.title: 1.5 mm² copper, out and back, carrying 10 A

visual.alt: A table showing the loop resistance of a five, thirty and fifty metre extension lead rising from about a tenth of an ohm to one point two, and the potential difference lost along it at ten amps rising from one volt to twelve

examples.title: How the car knows it is icy outside
examples.body:
The outside temperature on a car's dashboard, and the warning chime near freezing, come from a **thermistor** in the bumper or a mirror. Its resistance falls as it warms, steeply: a common one is 10 kΩ at 25 °C, about 33.6 kΩ at freezing and 3.6 kΩ on a hot day, nearly a tenfold change across the range.

The car's computer passes a small current through it, reads the pd, and $R = V \div I$ turns that into a temperature. A resistor that reacts is a sensor; the same idea with light in place of heat is the LDR you met in Year 10.

props.caption: One thermistor's resistance at three temperatures, drawn to scale.

visual.alt: Three bars drawn to scale showing a thermistor's resistance falling from about thirty four kilohms at freezing to ten at room temperature and under four on a hot day

examples.title: The diode inside every charger
examples.body:
The mains is alternating: the current reverses fifty times a second. A phone battery wants direct current, one way only. Between the two sits a **diode**, the component whose current–pd graph is flat on one side and rises on the other.

On the half of each cycle when the pd is the right way round, the diode's resistance is low and current flows to the battery. On the reversed half its resistance is very high and almost nothing gets through. The result is current in one direction, in pulses, which the rest of the charger smooths. The unsymmetrical graph the lesson draws is that job, one cycle at a time.

visual.alt: A table showing that a diode has a low resistance for the half of each mains cycle when the potential difference is the right way round, so current flows to the battery, and a very high resistance when it is reversed, so almost none does

steps.title: Current, potential difference and resistance
steps.body:
**Three quantities, and each one depends on the other two.**

**Current (I)** is the rate of flow of charge, measured in **amperes (A)**.

**Potential difference (V)** is the energy transferred per unit charge, measured in **volts (V)**. It is what pushes the current round.

**Resistance (R)** is how much a component opposes the current, measured in **ohms (Ω)**.

**The relationship the specification states:**

> The current through a component depends on **both** the resistance of the component **and** the potential difference across it. **The greater the resistance, the smaller the current** for a given potential difference.

That is the sentence to be able to write. The equation follows from it:

$$V = I R$$

**Recall and apply.** The specification requires you to **recall** this equation — it is not on the sheet, so it must be memorised, along with its rearrangements: $I = V \div R$ and $R = V \div I$.

**On wording.** Questions are set using **potential difference**, though you gain credit for either potential difference or voltage. Using the specification's term is the safer habit.

visuals.alt: An equation card giving V equals I R with its rearrangements for current and resistance, and the units of each quantity

check.prompt: A component of resistance 4 Ω has a potential difference of 12 V across it. What is the current, in amperes?

steps.title: Ohmic conductors
steps.body:
**Some components keep the same resistance; others do not.** The specification puts it as: for some resistors the value of **R remains constant**, but in others it **changes as the current changes**.

**An ohmic conductor at a constant temperature** is the simple case:

> The current through an ohmic conductor (at a constant temperature) is **directly proportional** to the potential difference across the resistor.

**Directly proportional** means double the pd and you double the current. On a graph of current against potential difference this gives a **straight line through the origin**, and the **resistance stays constant** as the current changes.

**The temperature condition matters.** A wire is ohmic **only while its temperature is constant**. Push enough current through it and it warms up, the resistance rises, and the proportionality fails — which is exactly what happens in a filament lamp.

**Reading a current–pd graph:**

- A **straight line through the origin** → resistance is **constant** → ohmic.
- A **curve** → resistance is **changing**.
- The **steeper** the line, the **lower** the resistance, since more current flows for the same pd.

That last point is the one to get right: a steep graph means a **small** resistance, not a large one.

check.prompt: What does a straight line through the origin on a current–potential difference graph show?
options: The resistance stays constant as the current changes
The resistance increases as the current increases
The component conducts in one direction only
The temperature of the component is rising
check.solution: A straight line through the origin means current is **directly proportional** to potential difference, so the **resistance is constant** — an ohmic conductor at constant temperature.

steps.title: Components whose resistance changes
steps.body:
**The specification names four components and what each one does.**

**The filament lamp.** As current increases the filament gets **hotter**, and **the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the temperature of the filament increases**. Its graph curves and **flattens** as pd rises, because each extra volt buys less extra current.

*Why:* a hotter metal has ions vibrating more, so electrons collide with them more often and find it harder to get through.

**The diode.** **Current through a diode flows in one direction only**, and it has a **very high resistance in the reverse direction**. Its graph is flat at almost zero on one side of the origin and rises steeply on the other.

**The thermistor.** **The resistance of a thermistor decreases as the temperature increases** — the opposite of a filament lamp. That makes it a temperature sensor: use it in a circuit and the current changes measurably as the room warms.

**The LDR (light dependent resistor).** Its resistance **decreases as light intensity increases**, which makes it a light sensor — for street lights that switch on at dusk, or a camera setting its exposure.

**The two sensors are worth learning as a pair**, because both work the same way: **more of the thing being sensed → less resistance → more current**. A thermistor senses heat, an LDR senses light.

**Watch the direction.** A filament lamp's resistance goes **up** with temperature; a thermistor's goes **down**. Both involve temperature, and mixing them up is the commonest error here.

steps.title: Investigating resistance
steps.body:
**Required practical 3** asks you to use circuit diagrams to set up and check circuits investigating the factors affecting resistance, covering **the length of a wire at constant temperature** and **combinations of resistors in series and parallel**.

**The circuit.** An **ammeter in series** with the wire measures the current through it. A **voltmeter in parallel** across the wire measures the potential difference. Resistance is then calculated with $R = V \div I$.

**Remember which goes where:** an ammeter measures what flows **through**, so it goes **in series**; a voltmeter measures the difference **across**, so it goes **in parallel**.

**The method for wire length.** Connect a length of wire, measure the current and pd, calculate the resistance, then repeat for several different lengths. Plot resistance against length.

**The result.** Resistance is **directly proportional to length** — a straight line through the origin. Double the length and you double the resistance, because the electrons have twice as far to travel against the same opposition.

**"At constant temperature" is doing real work in that sentence.** Current warms the wire, and a warmer wire has a **higher** resistance, which would spoil the result. So the circuit is **switched on only briefly** for each reading, and a low current is used. A question asking why the switch is opened between readings is asking exactly this.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Recall the equation.** $V = IR$ is **not** on the AQA equation sheet — the specification says students should be able to **recall and apply** it. The same is true of $P = VI$ and $P = I^2R$.

**Rearrange before substituting.** Write $R = V \div I$, then put the numbers in. Substituting first and rearranging afterwards is where most arithmetic errors are made, and it is much harder to spot them.

**Check by substituting back.** If $R = 30\ \Omega$ from 9 V and 0.3 A, then $0.3 \times 30 = 9$ ✓. Ten seconds, and it catches every rearrangement error.

**Be precise about proportionality.** *Directly proportional* means a **straight line through the origin** — not merely that one rises with the other. A filament lamp's current also rises with pd, and it is very much not proportional.

**Get the gradient the right way round.** A **steeper** line on a current–pd graph means a **lower** resistance, because more current flows for the same pd. Students routinely say the opposite.

**Explain the filament lamp with a mechanism.** Higher current → the filament gets **hotter** → the metal ions **vibrate more** → electrons **collide** with them more often → resistance **rises** → the graph flattens. A chain like that is worth far more than "it heats up".

**Keep the lamp and the thermistor apart.** A lamp's resistance **increases** with temperature; a thermistor's **decreases**. Both involve temperature, which is precisely why they are set together.

**Pair the two sensors.** A **thermistor** senses temperature and an **LDR** senses light, and both work the same way: more of the quantity → **less** resistance → **more** current. Saying that once explains both.

**Know why "at constant temperature" appears in the practical.** Current heats the wire and a hot wire has more resistance, so readings taken as it warms are not comparable. Switching on briefly is the control, and it is a favourite question.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Current (I)** is in **amperes**, **potential difference (V)** in **volts**, **resistance (R)** in **ohms**.
- **The greater the resistance, the smaller the current** for a given pd.
- **$V = IR$** — and you must **recall** it; it is not on the sheet.
- Rearranged: $I = V \div R$ and $R = V \div I$.
- Questions use **potential difference**; either term gains credit.
- An **ohmic conductor at constant temperature** has current **directly proportional** to pd.
- That gives a **straight line through the origin**, and **constant resistance**.
- A **curve** means the resistance is **changing**.
- A **steeper** line means a **lower** resistance.
- A **filament lamp**'s resistance **increases** as it gets hotter.
- A **diode** conducts **one way only**, with very high resistance in reverse.
- A **thermistor**'s resistance **decreases** as temperature increases.
- An **LDR**'s resistance **decreases** as light intensity increases.
- **Required practical 3**: ammeter in **series**, voltmeter in **parallel**, $R = V \div I$.
- Resistance is **directly proportional to the length** of a wire at constant temperature.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would investigate how the resistance of a wire depends on its length, and explain how you would make the investigation valid.
questions.solution:
**The circuit.** Connect a length of the test wire into a circuit with a battery or power supply and a switch. Place an **ammeter in series** with the wire, so it measures the current flowing **through** it, and a **voltmeter in parallel** across the wire, so it measures the potential difference **across** it. A variable resistor in series is useful for keeping the current low.

**The method.** Fix a metre rule alongside the wire and connect the circuit across a measured length — say 20 cm. Close the switch, take the ammeter and voltmeter readings quickly, then open it again. Calculate the resistance using $R = V \div I$.

Repeat for several different lengths — 20, 40, 60, 80 and 100 cm — taking readings at each. Then plot a graph of **resistance against length**.

**The expected result** is a **straight line through the origin**, showing that resistance is **directly proportional to length**: doubling the length doubles the resistance, because the electrons must travel twice as far against the same opposition.

**Making it valid.** The variable that must be controlled most carefully is **temperature**. Current passing through the wire **heats** it, and a hotter wire has a **higher resistance**. If the wire is allowed to warm up, a rise in resistance might be caused by the heating rather than by the extra length — so the experiment would no longer be testing what it claims to test.

There are two practical controls. First, **close the switch only briefly** for each reading and open it immediately afterwards, allowing the wire to cool between measurements. Second, keep the **current low**, using a variable resistor, since less current means less heating. The wire should be checked by touch, carefully, to confirm it is not warming.

Other variables to control are the **material** of the wire and its **thickness (cross-sectional area)**, both of which affect resistance — so the same reel of wire should be used throughout. The length should be measured from the same points on the crocodile clips each time, since a small error in length is proportionally large at 20 cm.

Finally, **repeat readings** at each length and take a mean, which reduces the effect of random error in reading the meters.

questions.prompt: A student plots current against potential difference for a resistor at constant temperature and for a filament lamp. Describe and explain the two graphs, and explain what each shows about resistance.
questions.solution:
**The resistor at constant temperature** gives a **straight line through the origin**. This shows that the current is **directly proportional** to the potential difference: doubling the pd doubles the current.

Because $R = V \div I$, and $V$ and $I$ rise in the same ratio, the **resistance is constant** however large the current becomes. This is what makes it an **ohmic conductor** — though only while the temperature really is held constant, which is why that condition is always stated.

**The filament lamp** gives a **curve** which is steep near the origin and **flattens** as the potential difference increases.

The explanation is a chain. As the pd rises, the current rises, and the current **heats the filament**. In a hotter metal the **ions vibrate more**, so the electrons flowing through **collide with them more often** and find it harder to pass. The **resistance therefore increases** with temperature.

Since $I = V \div R$ and $R$ is now larger, each extra volt produces **less** extra current than the volt before it — which is exactly what a flattening curve looks like. The lamp is **not** an ohmic conductor, because its resistance does not stay constant.

**Comparing them.** Near the origin the lamp's filament is still cool, so its graph is close to straight — the lamp behaves almost ohmically at very low currents and departs from it as it warms. That is a useful observation, because it shows the lamp is not a different kind of thing from the resistor; it is the same physics with the temperature no longer controlled.

**Reading resistance from either graph** is done the same way: take a point on the line, read off $V$ and $I$, and calculate $R = V \div I$. For the resistor any point gives the same answer; for the lamp the answer **depends which point you choose**, which is another way of saying the resistance is changing.

One comparison is easy to get backwards: a **steeper** line means **more current for the same pd**, and therefore a **lower** resistance. So where the lamp's curve has flattened, its resistance is at its highest.

**Comparing them.** Near the origin the lamp's filament is still cool, so its graph is close to straight — the lamp behaves almost ohmically at very low currents and departs from it as it warms. That is a useful observation, because it shows the lamp is not a different kind of thing from the resistor; it is the same physics with the temperature no longer controlled.

**Reading resistance from either graph** is done the same way: take a point on the line, read off $V$ and $I$, and calculate $R = V \div I$. For the resistor any point gives the same answer; for the lamp the answer **depends which point you choose**, which is another way of saying the resistance is changing.

One comparison is easy to get backwards: a **steeper** line means **more current for the same pd**, and therefore a **lower** resistance. So where the lamp's curve has flattened, its resistance is at its highest.

examTechnique.body:
**Recall $V = IR$** — it is not on the equation sheet. **Rearrange first, substitute second**, then check by putting the answer back in.

On a current–pd graph, **straight through the origin** means constant resistance, a **curve** means changing resistance, and a **steeper** line means **lower** resistance. Remember the lamp rises with temperature and the thermistor falls.
examinerErrors: Expecting V = IR to be given on the equation sheet.
Substituting into the equation before rearranging it.
Saying a steeper current–pd graph means higher resistance.
Describing a filament lamp as ohmic.
Saying a thermistor's resistance rises as it gets warmer.
Explaining the lamp graph as "it heats up" with no mechanism.
Putting the ammeter in parallel or the voltmeter in series.
Omitting temperature control from the resistance practical.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer **recalls** $V = IR$, rearranges **before** substituting, and checks the answer back. It uses *directly proportional* precisely, meaning a **straight line through the origin**, and reads gradients the right way round — **steeper is lower resistance**. It explains the filament lamp as a **chain**: hotter filament, ions vibrating more, more collisions, resistance rising, so each extra volt buys less current. It keeps the **lamp** and the **thermistor** moving in opposite directions, pairs the **thermistor and LDR** as sensors that both lose resistance as the sensed quantity rises, and knows that "**at constant temperature**" in the practical is a control with a reason behind it.
